activities.anchor: The constitution was admirable and unloved
activities.caption: pair each blow with the republic that took it
activities.name: gerWeimarMatch

config.prompt: Weimar's early storms — pair each with what it was:

pairs.right: ready-made blame for the civilians who signed the armistice
the threat from the left, crushed by Freikorps in January 1919
Ruhr passive resistance financed by the printing press, 1923

config.why: More than a dozen governments in fourteen years under proportional representation — yet the republic survived hyperinflation and two putsches, and the golden twenties gave Germany Bauhaus, modernist theatre and cinema on borrowed American money.

activities.anchor: the decision, from 1930, of conservative politicians
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the fatal ingredient
activities.name: gerPRPredict

config.q: Did proportional representation destroy Weimar — so that any republic with PR was doomed?
choices: Yes — the electoral maths was fatal wherever it was used
No — the republic survived six years of it and functioned when its elites wanted it to; the fatal ingredient came later
Yes — but only because of the hyperinflation
config.why: Democracy in Weimar died less by constitution than by abandonment — the men who ran the state stopped believing in it before the voters did.

activities.caption: read the curve — the peak of the misery
activities.name: gerPeakEstimate

config.prompt: Registered unemployment in Germany (annual average) peaked in 1932 at roughly how many millions?
config.why: 5.6 million on the annual average — over six million at the early-1932 peak, more than a third of the workforce — and the curve roughly quadrupled from 1928 to 1932 while the Nazi vote climbed with it.
config.context: Read the later fall sceptically: conscription and women removed from the statistics hid part of the recovery.

activities.caption: line up the vote shares, earliest first
activities.name: gerVoteOrder

config.prompt: The Nazi share of the vote — order these moments by date, earliest first:
items: 37.3 per cent — the largest bloc, July 1932
config.why: The rise tracked registered unemployment almost step for step — misery first, movement second — and the sequencing ends on a decline: the vote had already peaked when the Chancellery changed hands.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the control apparatus
activities.name: gerControlSpot

config.prompt: One line of this control-apparatus summary is wrong — click it:
lines: The SS and the Gestapo network ran the camps and the informers.
Goebbels's ministry ran radio sets into every front room from March 1933.
Rearmament, public works and the autobahn cut registered unemployment to near zero by 1938.
Dachau, the first concentration camp, opened in 1939.
Hitler Youth enrolment became compulsory in 1936.
config.correction: Dachau opened in March 1933 — within weeks of the takeover, for political opponents.
config.why: The Four-Year Plan (1936) pointed the economy at a war it could not afford peacefully — the apparatus reached everywhere, in doses of fear and consent historians still argue over.

activities.anchor: The experience depended entirely on who you were
activities.caption: file each detail under its group
activities.name: gerLifeBuckets

config.prompt: Everyday life in Nazi Germany — file each detail:

items.label: compulsory from 1936: camping, sport, ritual and indoctrination
the Edelweiss Pirates sang forbidden songs and mocked the uniforms
the White Rose leafleted against the war until the Scholls were executed
marriage loans (1933) paid couples to wed on condition the bride left work
the Mother's Cross: bronze for four children, silver for six, gold for eight
Strength Through Joy — cruises and theatre trips from the German Labour Front
five-mark weekly savings for a 'people's car' not one customer ever received

config.why: Real wages stayed below their 1929 level and the working week lengthened — prosperity was real, unevenly distributed, and partly an accounting of women, conscripts and political prisoners removed from the jobless totals.

activities.anchor: the confiscations and terror of Kristallnacht
activities.caption: call the share — the closing window
activities.name: gerEmigrationEstimate

config.prompt: By Kristallnacht (1938), roughly what share of Germany's roughly half-million Jews had emigrated?
config.why: More than half — through boycotts (April 1933), the Nuremberg Laws (1935) and the confiscations: for Jewish Germans the question of life in Nazi Germany had become escape or survival, and the remaining window was closing fast.

activities.caption: drag the divider — two books, one battalion
activities.name: gerMenCompare

config.prompt: The great argument about the perpetrators — drag the divider:

before.label: Browning, Ordinary Men (1992)
before.text: Middle-aged Hamburg workers shot tens of thousands in Poland in 1942 — conformity, careerism, alcohol and deference to authority, with no monsters among them.

after.label: Goldhagen, Hitler's Willing Executioners (1996)
after.text: 'Eliminationist' antisemitism was a German national culture all along — the counter-attack that packed lecture halls and forced the historiography to confront that the perpetrators were, overwhelmingly, unremarkable.

config.why: The controversy remains the field's great argument about how far explanation may drift toward exculpation.
